Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

ethical-principles.name: Ethical principles
ethical-principles.scope: Autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, conflicts of interest, financial incentives
ethical-principles.core: Four core pillars guide clinical ethics; patient welfare and transparency always override physician financial or personal interests.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Autonomy overrides beneficence** when a decisionally capable adult makes an informed refusal
Fiduciary duty: place **patient welfare above personal financial gain**

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Disclose conflicts of interest** (ownership, speaking fees, research funding) to patients
Ensure patients know **alternative referral options** when physician owns an imaging/surgery facility
Base clinical decisions solely on **medical necessity**, regardless of reimbursement model

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **Never accept gifts, meals, or kickbacks** from pharmaceutical or device companies
Never withhold indicated care or order unnecessary tests due to **financial incentives**

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Autonomy limited if patient **lacks capacity** or threatens public harm (e.g., active TB)
Double effect: **palliative opioids** risking respiratory depression are ethical when intent is comfort

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Disclosure alone does **not** excuse unethical self-referral or medically unnecessary procedures
Small nominal gifts (pens, lunches) still create bias and should be declined

ethical-principles.evidence: Not checked online; established AMA Code of Medical Ethics teaching.

extremity-vascular-injury.name: Extremity vascular injury
extremity-vascular-injury.scope: Hard signs (pulsatile bleeding, expanding hematoma, absent pulses, thrill/bruit, pallor), soft signs (diminished pulse, proximity), surgical exploration vs CT angiography
extremity-vascular-injury.core: After limb trauma, active arterial bleeding or threatened perfusion requires immediate intervention; stable equivocal findings require objective vascular assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Penetrating wounds near major vessels; blunt crush or traction injury
Knee dislocation, supracondylar humeral fracture, open fractures; spontaneous joint reduction may conceal mechanism

rows.label: Clues
items: Pain, pallor, coolness, paresthesia, paralysis indicate worsening ischemia; motor deficit is late
★ **Normal distal pulses do not exclude injury**, especially intimal tears after knee dislocation
Examine both limbs and document pulses, motor function, sensation before and after reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transection causes hemorrhage; intimal disruption → thrombosis and delayed ischemia
Contained arterial leak → pseudoaneurysm; artery–vein communication → traumatic AV fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hard signs → immediate **operative exploration**; imaging must not delay limb-saving treatment
Stable without hard signs → ABI/API; **<0.9** or abnormal examination → CT angiography
Normal examination + index ≥0.9 → serial examinations/follow-up; observe high-risk blunt injuries
Duplex ultrasound alternative in selected stable patients; CTA localizes injury for repair

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Direct pressure; uncontrolled hemorrhage → proximal tourniquet; avoid blind clamping
Resuscitate hemorrhagic shock with blood products; urgent vascular surgery consultation
★ Restore arterial flow rapidly, ideally within 6 hours; primary repair or vein graft
Temporary shunt when definitive repair delayed; coordinate fracture stabilization and revascularization
Prolonged ischemia, crush injury, marked swelling → early fasciotomy; monitor reperfusion hyperkalemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Amputation, persistent neuropathy, compartment syndrome; rhabdomyolysis and AKI after reperfusion
Delayed thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, graft infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Repeat neurovascular checks after splinting, reduction, and repair; promptly loosen constrictive dressings
Discharge follow-up essential for delayed swelling, recurrent bleeding, bruit, or new ischemic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Compartment syndrome: pain with passive stretch, tense compartments; pulses often remain palpable
Isolated nerve injury: focal deficits without objective perfusion abnormality

table.title: Trauma signs
rows: Absent pulses; bruit/thrill; overt distal ischemia
Diminished pulse; stable hematoma; prior bleeding

fetal-growth-restriction.name: Fetal growth restriction
fetal-growth-restriction.scope: Symmetric vs asymmetric FGR, uteroplacental insufficiency, chromosomal anomalies, congenital infections, umbilical artery Doppler surveillance, oligohydramnios
fetal-growth-restriction.core: Estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference below the 10th percentile requires evaluation for placental dysfunction and fetal disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal hypertension, preeclampsia, renal/vascular disease, smoking, cocaine, malnutrition, prior affected pregnancy
Aneuploidy, structural anomalies, CMV; multiple gestation

rows.label: Clues
items: Fundal height lag >3 cm, decreased movement, oligohydramnios; sometimes abnormal maternal placental disease markers
★ **EFW <3rd percentile** indicates severe disease; normal-size parents do not establish constitutional smallness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental resistance reduces oxygen/nutrients; redistribution preserves cerebral over abdominal growth
Low fetal renal perfusion reduces urine production and fluid volume

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ultrasound biometry using reliable dating → detailed anatomy; serial growth generally every 3–4 weeks
★ **Umbilical artery Doppler every 1–2 weeks**; absent (AEDV)/reversed (REDV) diastolic velocity → intensified surveillance
Weekly NST after viability; increase frequency with Doppler deterioration or maternal comorbidity
Early <32 weeks, unexplained or anomalous → offer amniocentesis/microarray; CMV PCR if amniocentesis chosen
Do not order indiscriminate TORCH panels without exposure or suggestive findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reversed flow → **hospitalization**, corticosteroids, frequent cardiotocography, delivery planning
Anticipated preterm birth → betamethasone; magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 32 weeks
Nonreassuring testing/maternal deterioration → earlier delivery; absent/reversed flow may favor cesarean
Bed rest, sildenafil, and LMWH solely to treat/prevent FGR provide no established benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Stillbirth, intrapartum intolerance, neonatal hypoglycemia, hypothermia, polycythemia; later metabolic/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Tobacco/drug cessation, maternal disease control; low-dose aspirin when preeclampsia-risk criteria met

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incorrect dates: early ultrasound establishes gestational age
Constitutionally small fetus: reassuring interval growth and normal Doppler without placental disease

table.title: Patterns and delivery in otherwise stable disease
rows: Often later placental insufficiency; patterns overlap

foodborne-illnesses.name: Foodborne illnesses
foodborne-illnesses.scope: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, scombroid, ciguatera, Salmonella, Campylobacter
foodborne-illnesses.core: Incubation time and the dominant symptom separate preformed-toxin vomiting from intestinal infection requiring selective stool testing and antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Food improperly refrigerated/reheated; shared-meal outbreaks; raw poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat
Infancy, older age, immunosuppression or vascular disease increase invasive Salmonella risk
Improperly chilled tuna/mackerel → scombroid; tropical reef fish → ciguatera

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt short-lived emesis without fever favors ingested toxin; inflammatory enteritis → fever or bloody stools
★ **Severe dehydration, bacteremia signs or persistent bloody diarrhea** → urgent assessment
Campylobacter pain may mimic appendicitis; poultry exposure supports both major invasive enteric pathogens
Fish toxins: scombroid → flushing/urticaria; ciguatera → paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ingested enterotoxins act rapidly; scombroid: histamine; ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels
Invasive mucosal infection induces inflammation and can permit bloodstream spread
S aureus: **heat-stable** preformed enterotoxin builds in unrefrigerated food; cooking does not destroy it

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild brief outbreak illness → **clinical diagnosis**, usually no stool studies
Fever, bloody/mucoid stool, severe tenderness or sepsis → stool PCR/culture including Shiga toxin testing
Suspected bacteremia → blood cultures; report suspected outbreaks to public health

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scombroid → **diphenhydramine/famotidine**; anaphylaxis → epinephrine; ciguatera → supportive care
Oral rehydration; severe dehydration → IV isotonic fluids; toxin syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics
Campylobacter severe/prolonged or high-risk illness → azithromycin; most mild cases resolve untreated
Nontyphoidal Salmonella: severe/invasive or high-risk host → ceftriaxone or susceptibility-directed antibiotic
★ Suspected **STEC → avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs**; hemolytic uremic syndrome risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Campylobacter → Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis; Salmonella → bacteremia, vascular infection, sickle-cell osteomyelitis
Volume depletion → AKI; antibiotics may prolong uncomplicated Salmonella carriage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cook poultry/eggs thoroughly; separate raw foods, rapid refrigeration, handwashing; avoid unpasteurized products

rows.label: Mimics
items: Norovirus: contagious outbreak with vomiting and diarrhea
Appendicitis: focal progressive peritoneal findings; toxin illness usually self-limited

foodborne-illnesses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC marine toxins](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html), CDC Salmonella/Campylobacter and IDSA infectious-diarrhea guidance.

table.title: Timing after exposure
rows: Vomiting; cream pastries, mayonnaise salads, handled meats

foreign-body-aspiration.name: Foreign body aspiration
foreign-body-aspiration.scope: Pediatric airway foreign body, choking maneuvers, rigid bronchoscopy, chest x-ray findings (air trapping, atelectasis), observation of partial obstruction
foreign-body-aspiration.core: Abrupt choking with unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests airway foreign body, even with normal radiographs.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Children <3 years exploring objects orally; nuts, seeds, grapes, hot dogs, toy fragments
Neurologic swallowing impairment, sedation, intoxication, poor dentition in adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed coughing/gagging during eating or play; symptoms may partially resolve after initial event
★ **Cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe** → severe airway obstruction
Proximal obstruction: stridor; distal obstruction: focal wheeze, persistent cough, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia
Cyanosis, altered consciousness, exhaustion → imminent respiratory arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Partial ball-valve blockage allows inspiration but limits expiration → distal hyperinflation
Complete bronchial blockage → resorption atelectasis; retained organic material causes inflammation and infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable child → **chest x-ray**, including expiratory or bilateral decubitus views when feasible
Unilateral air trapping, mediastinal shift, collapse, or radiopaque object may identify location
Most food objects are radiolucent; negative examination/imaging does not exclude a convincing history
★ High suspicion → **bronchoscopy**; avoid delaying definitive evaluation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: Effective cough/partial obstruction → encourage coughing, observe closely; no blind finger sweep
★ Infant severe choking: **5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts**, repeat
Age ≥1 year: cycles of five back blows/five abdominal thrusts; pregnancy/marked obesity → chest thrusts
Unresponsive → CPR, inspect mouth during airway opening, remove visible object only
★ Stable retained pediatric object → **rigid bronchoscopy** for retrieval; expert airway team for unstable obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrest, postobstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, granulation tissue
Removal can cause bleeding, edema, or pneumothorax; persistent symptoms need reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid small hard foods/toys; cut grapes lengthwise, supervise eating, avoid running with food
Teach caregivers choking response; keep small objects away from young children

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent diffuse wheeze with bronchodilator response
Croup: preceding URI, barking cough, diffuse upper-airway obstruction
Bronchiolitis: viral prodrome, diffuse crackles/wheezing in an infant

gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
gastroenteritis.scope: Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus), foodborne illness, bacterial enteritis, traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), oral rehydration therapy, dehydration assessment
gastroenteritis.core: Acute vomiting and diarrhea usually need hydration and selective testing; shock, blood, focal pain, or systemic toxicity changes the approach.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, childcare or institutional outbreaks
Infants, older adults and immunocompromised people have greater dehydration or invasive-infection risk
Pet reptiles → nontyphoidal Salmonella; young infants prone to bacteremia

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools and diffuse cramps favor noninvasive disease; fever or dysentery suggests inflammatory enteritis
Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine; children → fewer wet diapers, absent tears
★ Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension → **severe dehydration/shock**
Toddler + high fever, bloody diarrhea, **seizure** → Shigella; HUS appears days later with hemolysis/AKI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal secretion or epithelial injury causes water/electrolyte losses
Sodium–glucose cotransport remains functional, allowing oral rehydration despite ongoing diarrhea

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild self-limited illness → **no routine stool tests**
Stool PCR/culture and Shiga toxin for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe pain or sepsis
Electrolytes/creatinine for severe dehydration; C difficile testing after antibiotics or healthcare exposure
Persistent >14 days or relevant travel → evaluate parasites; focal/peritoneal pain → imaging for surgical cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral rehydration solution**, frequent small volumes; continue breastfeeding and usual diet
Shock/severe dehydration or failed oral intake → IV isotonic crystalloid; reassess perfusion
Ondansetron can enable oral hydration; avoid juice/soda as primary replacement
Moderate/severe travelers’ diarrhea → azithromycin; suspected STEC → no antibiotics
Loperamide only selected adults with afebrile nonbloody diarrhea; avoid children and inflammatory disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities; postinfectious lactose intolerance
STEC → HUS with hemolysis, low platelets and AKI; invasive bacteria → bacteremia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap/water, food safety, **rotavirus vaccination** in infancy
Norovirus outbreaks: environmental disinfection; food handlers remain off work ≥48 hours after symptoms resolve

rows.label: Mimics
items: Appendicitis/intussusception: localized or episodic severe pain disproportionate to diarrhea
DKA: hyperglycemia, ketones; IBD: persistent bloody diarrhea and weight loss

table.title: Common noninvasive enteritis
rows: Vomiting followed by substantial watery diarrhea

generalized-anxiety-disorder.name: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
generalized-anxiety-disorder.scope: GAD diagnostic criteria, pharmacotherapy (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone), psychotherapy (CBT), differential diagnosis
generalized-anxiety-disorder.core: Difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday domains on most days for at least 6 months causes distress or functional impairment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family anxiety history, chronic stress, trauma, female sex, comorbid depression
Caffeine, stimulants, thyroid hormone excess, and substance withdrawal can reproduce symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Adults: **≥3** of restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance
Children require only one associated symptom; reassurance provides limited sustained relief
Worries shift among health, family, work, and finances rather than one circumscribed trigger
Assess suicidality, substance use, depressive symptoms, and manic history before treatment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heightened threat appraisal and impaired fear regulation perpetuate autonomic arousal and anticipatory worry
Avoidance and reassurance-seeking reinforce anxiety, providing targets for cognitive and behavioral interventions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** after excluding substance effects and medical explanations
GAD-7 quantifies severity and response; not a substitute for diagnostic interview
TSH, ECG, or other testing guided by tremor, weight change, palpitations, or examination
Symptoms confined to another disorder, such as obsessions or trauma reminders, favor that diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CBT** targets cognitive distortions, avoidance, and worry; exercise and sleep regularity support recovery
★ Persistent impairment → **SSRI** such as escitalopram/sertraline, or SNRI such as venlafaxine/duloxetine
Buspirone: scheduled nonbenzodiazepine option; delayed onset, low dependence risk, not useful as needed
Allow several weeks at therapeutic dose; continue effective treatment after remission, then taper gradually
Benzodiazepines: brief selected bridging only; avoid chronic use, especially with opioids or fall risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Depression, impaired function, substance misuse; benzodiazepine dependence and withdrawal
SSRIs/SNRIs: GI effects, sexual dysfunction, early activation; SNRIs may increase BP

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce caffeine/stimulants, practice CBT skills, monitor relapse during medication taper
Address chronic stress and comorbid sleep, mood, or substance-use disorders

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: discrete abrupt attacks with anticipatory fear
Adjustment disorder: stressor-linked symptoms beginning within 3 months
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, suppressed TSH

generalized-anxiety-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established psychiatric diagnostic and treatment teaching.

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.name: Gestational trophoblastic disease
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.scope: Complete hydatidiform mole, partial hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma, suction curettage, serial beta-hCG surveillance, contraception
gestational-trophoblastic-disease.core: Abnormal trophoblastic proliferation causes excessive hCG, bleeding, and vesicular placental tissue; persistent hCG after evacuation suggests gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior molar pregnancy, extremes of reproductive age; choriocarcinoma can follow any pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Vaginal bleeding, hyperemesis, uterus larger than dates, bilateral theca lutein cysts
★ **Preeclampsia before 20 weeks** or gestational thyrotoxicosis → suspect mole
Postpregnancy bleeding with cough/hemoptysis or neurologic symptoms → metastatic trophoblastic malignancy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal fertilization produces proliferative hydropic villi; high hCG stimulates thyroid and ovarian receptors
Choriocarcinoma lacks chorionic villi and spreads hematogenously, especially to lungs, vagina, brain

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Quantitative **β-hCG + pelvic ultrasound**; snowstorm/multicystic placental appearance may be absent early
Evacuated tissue histopathology confirms; p57 absent in complete mole, retained in partial mole
★ Postevacuation **hCG plateau over 3 weeks or rise over 2 weeks** → evaluate GTN
Suspected neoplasia → chest imaging and stage/risk assessment; avoid biopsy of vascular vaginal metastasis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stabilize bleeding → **suction curettage**; send tissue; give anti-D if Rh-negative
Hysterectomy an option when fertility not desired; surveillance remains necessary
Low-risk GTN → methotrexate or actinomycin D; high-risk → multiagent chemotherapy
hCG every 1–2 weeks until normal; partial: reconfirm after 1 month; complete: monthly for 6 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, thyroid storm, early hypertensive disease, invasive mole, metastatic malignancy
Chemotherapy toxicity; prognosis often excellent even with metastatic disease when treated

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reliable contraception during hCG surveillance; combined OCPs acceptable; defer pregnancy until follow-up complete
Future pregnancy → early ultrasound and postpregnancy hCG assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Multiple gestation: high hCG with recognizable normally developing fetuses
Missed abortion: nonviable gestation without trophoblastic overgrowth

table.title: Molar subtypes
rows: Usually triploid; maternal + two paternal sets

gestational-trophoblastic-disease.evidence: Surveillance checked 2026-10-30: [FIGO 2025 update](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12411817/); remaining pathology established teaching.

glaucoma.name: Glaucoma
glaucoma.scope: Open-angle glaucoma, acute angle-closure glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure, optic disc cupping, tonometry, visual field testing, topical prostaglandins, laser trabeculoplasty, iridotomy
glaucoma.core: Progressive optic nerve damage threatens vision; a sudden painful red eye from angle closure is an emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Open-angle: older age, family history, African ancestry, myopia, chronic glucocorticoids
Angle closure: shallow chamber, hyperopia, aging lens, pharmacologic dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Open-angle: central acuity preserved until late
★ Acute closure: halos, vomiting, hazy cornea, **fixed mid-dilated pupil**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Open-angle: trabecular outflow resistance despite patent angle
Pupillary block → bowed iris obstructs trabecular meshwork → rapid IOP rise

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Tonometry** measures IOP; normal pressure does not exclude glaucoma
**Gonioscopy** determines angle anatomy
Disc exam/OCT: increased cup-to-disc ratio, rim thinning, retinal nerve fiber loss
Automated perimetry: nasal step or arcuate scotoma; serial testing tracks progression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute closure: urgent ophthalmology; acetazolamide plus topical timolol and brimonidine; IV mannitol if refractory
Pilocarpine after IOP falls in pupillary block; delay definitive laser until cornea clears
Open-angle progression despite maximal tolerated therapy → consider filtration surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible optic nerve damage and blindness
Latanoprost: iris darkening and eyelash growth

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prophylactic iridotomy in fellow eye after primary acute closure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anterior uveitis: small pupil, consensual photophobia, anterior chamber cells
Conjunctivitis: discharge, preserved acuity, minimal pain

glaucoma.evidence: Checked AAO Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2025).

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.scope: Nephritic syndrome, poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GN (anti-GBM, ANCA), lupus nephritis, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria quantification, kidney biopsy
glomerulonephritis.core: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced filtration; rapidly rising creatinine demands urgent evaluation for crescentic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis/skin infection, systemic autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculitis
IgA nephropathy often follows mucosal infection; anti-GBM pulmonary bleeding risk increases with smoking

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs** identify a glomerular bleeding source
Tea-colored urine, oliguria, periorbital swelling; nephrotic-range protein loss can coexist
★ **Hemoptysis + AKI** → pulmonary–renal syndrome; rapidly progressive disease may initially lack systemic symptoms

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune complexes, basement-membrane antibodies, or pauci-immune vascular injury inflame glomerular capillaries
Crescent formation compresses capillary tufts → rapid, potentially irreversible loss of filtration
Reduced filtration → sodium/water retention → **volume overload**, edema, hypertension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urinalysis/microscopy → **creatinine, electrolytes, urine protein/creatinine ratio**; monitor urine output
C3/C4, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM; ASO/anti-DNase B when poststreptococcal disease suspected
★ **Kidney biopsy** for rapidly progressive AKI, substantial persistent proteinuria, or uncertain systemic GN
Typical childhood poststreptococcal course may not require biopsy; persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks warrants reassessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Salt restriction, loop diuretics for overload, BP control; ACE inhibitor/ARB for persistent proteinuria when stable
★ Pulmonary–renal/RPGN → **urgent nephrology, steroids + immunosuppression** before irreversible decline
Anti-GBM: plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide; ANCA: rituximab/cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange only selected severe cases
Lupus: biopsy-directed mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide + steroids; poststreptococcal disease mainly supportive

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, CKD; dialysis for refractory life-threatening derangements
Immunosuppression → infection, cytopenias, infertility with cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP/proteinuria, avoid nephrotoxins, follow renal function and urine findings

rows.label: Mimics
items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

gonococcal-infection.name: Gonococcal infection
gonococcal-infection.scope: Urethritis/cervicitis, disseminated gonococcal infection, gonococcal arthritis, neonatal conjunctivitis
gonococcal-infection.core: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes mucosal infection and can disseminate into a dermatitis-tenosynovitis-arthritis syndrome or purulent septic arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: New/multiple partners, inconsistent barriers, prior STI, younger age
Complement deficiency increases dissemination risk; neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix; rectal/pharyngeal disease often asymptomatic
★ **Migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules** → disseminated infection
Neonate: copious purulent conjunctivitis 2–5 days after birth; corneal injury can progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci adhere to mucosa; antigenic variation permits recurrent infection
Ascending genital spread or bacteremia extends disease beyond initial exposure site

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT at exposed sites**: urine/vaginal, rectal, pharyngeal; test chlamydia, HIV, syphilis
Symptomatic male urethral Gram stain may show intracellular diplococci; less reliable at other sites
Dissemination: blood/synovial cultures and mucosal NAAT; negative joint culture does not exclude diagnosis
Suspected treatment failure → culture and antimicrobial susceptibility, assess reinfection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated: **ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once**; ≥150 kg → 1 g once
Chlamydia not excluded → doxycycline 7 days, don't await results; pregnancy, older exam questions → azithromycin
★ Disseminated disease → **IV/IM ceftriaxone**, hospitalization initially; drain purulent joint
Neonatal infection → systemic ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime if bilirubin/calcium concerns; topical treatment alone insufficient

rows.label: Complications
items: PID, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, epididymitis, corneal perforation
Rare endocarditis/meningitis; untreated septic arthritis damages cartilage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; abstain 7 days after treatment and until partners treated
Retest at 3 months; pharyngeal test-of-cure at 7–14 days; routine urogenital test-of-cure unnecessary
Condoms, risk-based screening; neonatal erythromycin eye ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chlamydia: similar urethritis/cervicitis, NAAT distinguishes
Reactive arthritis: sterile arthritis after infection, conjunctivitis/enthesitis
Staphylococcal arthritis: usually isolated hot joint without migratory skin-tendon syndrome

graft-versus-host-disease.name: Graft-versus-host disease
graft-versus-host-disease.scope: Acute GVHD (maculopapular rash, secretory diarrhea, hyperbilirubinemia), chronic GVHD (sclerotic skin, lichenoid changes, sicca syndrome), donor T-cell mediated attack, methylprednisolone
graft-versus-host-disease.core: Multisystem injury from donor immune cells after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: HLA mismatch, unrelated donor, older recipient, peripheral blood graft; prior acute disease increases chronic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Acute: rash often begins on face, ears, palms or soles; severe cases blister or desquamate
★ Chronic: reduced joint range from fasciitis; new airflow obstruction suggests bronchiolitis obliterans

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Donor **T cells** recognize recipient alloantigens; epithelial injury acutely, dysregulated immunity and fibrosis chronically

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classify by manifestations; day 100 alone does not distinguish acute from chronic disease
Stage acute disease by rash extent, bilirubin, and diarrhea volume or severe GI symptoms
Exclude infection and drug toxicity; biopsy affected tissue when uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: Limited skin disease → topical corticosteroids; supportive fluids, nutrition and infection surveillance
★ Significant acute disease → systemic **methylprednisolone**
Moderate or severe chronic disease → systemic prednisone; steroid-refractory acute or chronic disease → ruxolitinib

rows.label: Complications
items: Fluid and protein loss, skin contractures, irreversible airflow obstruction, opportunistic infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Post-transplant cyclophosphamide or calcineurin inhibitor-based prophylaxis by transplant protocol
Irradiated cellular blood products for at-risk recipients prevent transfusion-associated GVHD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome: painful hepatomegaly, weight gain and ascites early after transplant
C difficile colitis: toxin-positive stool without characteristic skin or liver involvement

graft-versus-host-disease.evidence: Checked EBMT consensus recommendations on GVHD prophylaxis and management (2024).

health-care-delivery-and-insurance.name: Health care delivery and insurance
health-care-delivery-and-insurance.scope: Insurance coverage denials and appeals, prior authorization, managed care, Medicare and Medicaid, uninsured access
health-care-delivery-and-insurance.core: Advocate for medically necessary care through appeals and assistance programs without falsifying records or abandoning uninsured patients.

rows.label: Principle
items: **EMTALA**: EDs must **stabilize every patient** regardless of insurance or ability to pay

rows.label: Do
items: ★ IF insurer denies indicated care → **appeal with clinical justification** (peer-to-peer review)
★ Obtain **prior authorization** for non-urgent costly care; offer generic alternatives
For **uninsured** patients → connect to **social work**, Medicaid enrollment, or safety-net clinics

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **Never falsify diagnoses or upcode** to obtain insurance coverage or approval
Never withhold discussing an indicated treatment solely because insurance may not cover it

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Emergent life-saving care proceeds immediately; never delay stabilization for insurer approval

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Never tell patients to **pay out of pocket** without appealing or exploring alternatives
Managed care cost constraints never justify **gag clauses** or hiding treatment options

table.title: US insurance & payment models
rows: Fixed fee per patient per month

health-care-delivery-and-insurance.evidence: Not checked online; established US health systems teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles or wheeze (cardiac asthma), dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Low effective volume → baroreceptor-driven nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease
Alveolar flooding → V/Q mismatch, widened A-a gradient, hypoxemia
High-output HF: severe anemia, AV fistula (larger fistula → more shunt); HF signs with **normal/high EF**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Congested HFrEF → loop diuretic + **ACE inhibitor/ARNI first**; beta-blocker/MRA once compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI: 36-hour washout
MRA: eGFR >30, K <5; never ACE inhibitor + ARB; EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD
HFrEF foundation drugs lower mortality; loop diuretics, nitrates alone, digoxin relieve symptoms only

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain
ARDS: diffuse infiltrates, no cephalization; massive crystalloid + **cephalization/perihilar fullness** → volume overload

table.title: Chronic phenotypes
rows: Sacubitril/valsartan (or ACEi/ARB), carvedilol/metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, dapagliflozin

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

herpes-simplex-virus.name: Herpes simplex virus
herpes-simplex-virus.scope: HSV-1 and HSV-2, genital herpes, neonatal herpes, herpes labialis, eczema herpeticum, acyclovir
herpes-simplex-virus.core: Painful grouped vesicles recurring at mucocutaneous sites reflect latent HSV reactivation; neonatal infection and disseminated disease require urgent systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin/mucosal contact, asymptomatic shedding, new sexual partners; either HSV type can cause genital disease
Immunosuppression, atopic dermatitis; neonatal risk highest with newly acquired maternal infection near delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary genital: fever, tender nodes, dysuria, painful ulcers, 2–3 weeks; recurrences milder, resolve within 1 week
Labialis: tingling prodrome, vermilion cluster; **whitlow**: painful grouped finger vesicles after oral-secretion exposure
★ **Monomorphic punched-out erosions in eczema** → eczema herpeticum; ocular symptoms threaten vision
Neonate: sepsislike illness, vesicles sometimes absent; seizures/hepatitis suggest CNS or disseminated disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV establishes sensory ganglion latency; stress, illness, UV exposure trigger reactivation
Genital HSV-2 recurs/sheds more than genital HSV-1

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active lesion → **HSV PCR/NAAT with typing**; culture less sensitive as lesions heal
Encephalitis/neonatal CNS concern, **lymphocytic CSF with RBCs** → CSF HSV PCR; early negative may require repeat
Neonate → lesion/surface, blood, CSF testing plus liver enzymes; treat while testing
No routine type-specific serology screening or HSV IgM

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First genital episode → **oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7–10 days**; start before results
Recurrence → prompt episodic dosing at prodrome; frequent/distressing episodes → daily suppressive valacyclovir
★ Neonatal, CNS, disseminated disease or severe eczema herpeticum → **IV acyclovir**
Pregnancy: acyclovir/valacyclovir from 36 weeks; labor lesions/prodrome → cesarean; neither → vaginal despite history
Corneal involvement → urgent ophthalmology; avoid unsupervised ocular corticosteroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, urinary retention, keratitis, dissemination; increased HIV acquisition risk
Acyclovir → crystal nephropathy, neurotoxicity with renal impairment; hydrate, adjust dose

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Avoid sex during lesions/prodrome**, condoms, partner disclosure; suppression lowers but never eliminates transmission
Avoid kissing infants with active labialis; cover lesions, hand hygiene

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syphilis: classically painless chancre; chancroid: deep purulent painful ulcer
Aphthae: mucosal ulcers, no preceding vesicles
Zoster: unilateral dermatomal eruption
Felon/paronychia: pus, no vesicles; whitlow → oral acyclovir, **no incision/drainage**

herpes-simplex-virus.evidence: Checked genital disease 2026-10-30: [CDC HSV guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/herpes.htm); neonatal/eczema management established teaching.

table.title: Neonatal IV acyclovir duration
rows: ≥21 days; CNS: confirm CSF PCR clearance

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection 2–4 weeks post-exposure: fever, rash, sore throat, **mucosal ulcers**, diarrhea, generalized lymphadenopathy
Weight loss, thrush, recurrent candida/herpes, **extensive adult molluscum** → test HIV; dysphagia → candidal esophagitis
Child/teen: chronic fever/diarrhea, poor growth, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB, pregnancy testing, **cervical cytology**
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count
Prenatal: opt-out screening; refusal → counsel, re-offer later; never test without consent

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: **pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin**, else TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, ophthalmology
Untreated/viremic mother's newborn → **triple ART** ASAP, ideally within 6 h, ≤6 weeks; suppressed mother → zidovudine alone

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary lesion; biopsy after failed empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment, earlier if serology/imaging/CSF PCR disagree
SCID/CVID: low immunoglobulins; SCID lymphopenia, no nodes; perinatal HIV: PJP, thrush, nodes, normal lymphocytes

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; sputum/BAL silver stain
Ring-enhancing mass lesions, edema/mass effect; positive IgG
Cognitive decline; non-enhancing subcortical demyelination, no mass effect

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation
High filtered calcium exceeds tubular reabsorption → **hypercalciuria** → calcium stones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **Denosumab** (favored, esp renal limitation/refractory) or **IV zoledronic acid/pamidronate** for sustained malignancy control
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.scope: Bird fancier lung, farmer lung, acute vs chronic presentation, antigen avoidance, centrilobular ground-glass nodules on HRCT, systemic corticosteroids
hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.core: Immune-mediated small-airway and interstitial lung disease follows inhaled antigen exposure; identifying and removing the exposure is central to treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Bird proteins from pets, feathers, droppings; moldy hay in farming
Damp buildings, contaminated humidifiers/hot tubs, occupational organic dust; ask about home and hobbies

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **cough, dyspnea, fever hours after exposure**, improvement away from source
Chronic exposure: insidious exertional limitation, weight loss, dry inspiratory crackles; clubbing with fibrosis
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, falling exercise saturation indicate substantial impairment; chronic disease may lack febrile episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Repeated antigen inhalation triggers immune-complex and T-cell responses around bronchioles and alveoli
Persistent inflammation produces poorly formed noncaseating granulomas and potentially irreversible fibrosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Exposure history + HRCT**: centrilobular ground-glass nodules, mosaic attenuation, expiratory air trapping
Fibrotic disease: reticulation, traction bronchiectasis ± honeycombing; distribution can differ from basal-predominant IPF
PFTs: restriction and ↓DLCO, sometimes mixed obstruction; BAL lymphocytosis supports diagnosis
Serum antigen-specific IgG documents sensitization, **not disease**; absence does not exclude
Multidisciplinary review; biopsy only when exposure, imaging, and BAL leave clinically important uncertainty

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Complete antigen avoidance** and environmental remediation; respirator alone may be insufficient
★ Severe symptomatic nonfibrotic disease → **systemic glucocorticoids** to accelerate recovery
Oxygen for hypoxemia, pulmonary rehabilitation; progressive fibrotic disease → specialist antifibrotic consideration
Advanced refractory fibrosis → lung transplant evaluation; antibiotics do not treat sterile immune inflammation

rows.label: Complications
items: Progressive fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic respiratory failure, cor pulmonale
Symptoms can persist despite avoidance once irreversible structural damage has occurred

rows.label: Prevention
items: Remove birds/mold sources, maintain ventilation, control workplace organic-dust exposure
Counsel household members about ongoing feather products or hidden dampness; monitor lung function after removal

rows.label: Mimics
items: IPF: older adult, basal subpleural honeycombing, no explanatory antigen
Sarcoidosis: well-formed granulomas, hilar adenopathy, extrapulmonary involvement
Organic dust toxic syndrome: heavy exposure, acute flu-like illness without antigen-specific sensitization

hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.evidence: Not checked online; established ATS diagnostic and management teaching.

hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.name: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.scope: Chronic and gestational HTN, preeclampsia, HELLP, eclampsia
hypertensive-disorders-of-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy-associated hypertension; maternal organ injury or placental dysfunction signals danger even without substantial proteinuria.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior preeclampsia, chronic HTN, CKD, diabetes, SLE/APS, multifetal gestation
Nulliparity, obesity, age ≥35, family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, visual disturbance, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea; edema nonspecific
★ Severe features: **platelets <100,000/µL**, creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubled, transaminases ≥2× normal
Other severe features: pulmonary edema, refractory neurologic symptoms
Presentation through **6 weeks postpartum**; eclampsia/HELLP possible without prior HTN

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal spiral-artery remodeling → placental ischemia → systemic endothelial injury, vasospasm, capillary leak

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **BP ≥140/90**, either component, twice ≥4 h apart; severe ≥160/110 confirmed within minutes
CBC/platelets, creatinine, AST/ALT, urine protein; fetal growth US + antenatal testing
Proteinuria: **≥300 mg/24 h** or protein/creatinine ≥0.3; dipstick 2+ only if quantification unavailable
Chronic HTN + new proteinuria/end-organ injury → superimposed preeclampsia; HELLP: smear, LDH ≥600 IU/L

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Persistent severe BP ≥15 min → **IV labetalol/hydralazine** or immediate-release oral nifedipine within 30–60 min
★ Severe preeclampsia/eclampsia → **magnesium sulfate** through 24 h postpartum; airway before delivery
Chronic HTN ≥140/90 → oral labetalol/extended-release nifedipine; avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs
Mg toxicity: areflexia/hypoventilation → stop infusion, **IV calcium gluconate**; oliguria → reduce dose

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, abruption, DIC, AKI, hepatic hematoma/rupture; fetal growth restriction, prematurity, death

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High risk or multiple moderate risks → **aspirin 81 mg/day**, start 12–28 wk, ideally before 16
Postpartum BP review within 72 h if severe, otherwise 7–10 days; long-term cardiovascular follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: TTP: profound thrombocytopenia/hemolysis, persists after delivery
Acute fatty liver: hypoglycemia, jaundice, marked coagulopathy
Epilepsy: established seizure disorder; evaluate alternative causes despite obstetric context

table.title: Classification and delivery
rows: Before 20 wk or persists >12 wk postpartum
After 20 wk + proteinuria OR severe features
Severe BP alone sufficient; <34 stable → betamethasone
Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets
Deliver after stabilization, any gestational age

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, lid lag, onycholysis, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults: apathetic
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → **Doppler ultrasound** or radioiodine uptake (not if pregnant/lactating)
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, mild hypercalcemia, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity
Pregnancy: thionamides/TRAb cross placenta → **fetal goiter**, impaired swallowing, polyhydramnios

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing
Orbital pseudotumor: involves muscle bellies and tendons; Graves spares tendons

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema, acropachy (clubbing)
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hypoglycemia.name: Hypoglycemia
hypoglycemia.scope: Drug-induced hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), Whipple triad, acute management (dextrose, glucagon), insulinoma
hypoglycemia.core: Compatible symptoms, documented low plasma glucose, and relief with correction establish Whipple triad and justify evaluation for a hypoglycemic disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Insulin, sulfonylureas; missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney failure increase risk
Sepsis, liver failure, adrenal insufficiency; insulinoma causes fasting episodes in otherwise well adults
Child, illness, poor intake or sugar-free fluids → **glycogen depletion**, ketotic hypoglycemia ± anion-gap acidosis

rows.label: Clues
items: Adrenergic: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger; neuroglycopenic: confusion, visual change, seizures, coma
Autonomic neuropathy or recurrent episodes may blunt warning symptoms
★ Glucose **<54 mg/dL** clinically significant; diabetes alert threshold <70 mg/dL

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Excess insulin suppresses glucose output and ketones; substrate/hormone deficits impair counterregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside glucose immediately**; plasma confirmation if discordant, never delay emergency correction
Critical sample: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen
Suspected endogenous fasting disorder → supervised fast up to 72 h; mixed-meal test for postprandial symptoms
Biochemically confirmed insulinoma → pancreatic CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound if localization unclear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Awake and swallowing → **15 g rapid carbohydrate**, recheck after 15 minutes, repeat if needed
★ Altered or unable to swallow → **IV dextrose**; no IV access → IM/intranasal glucagon
After recovery → longer-acting carbohydrate; glucagon less effective after alcohol or glycogen depletion
★ Sulfonylurea recurrence → **octreotide + dextrose**, prolonged observation; long-acting insulin may require infusion
Adjust diabetes regimen and treat trigger; localized insulinoma → surgical resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Seizures, brain injury, arrhythmias, falls; recurrent episodes cause impaired awareness
Dextrose alone after sulfonylurea exposure may stimulate further insulin release

rows.label: Prevention
items: Meal/exercise planning, glucose monitoring or CGM alarms, caregiver rescue-glucagon education
Relax overly intensive targets when recurrent events, frailty, or impaired awareness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic attack: normal glucose during symptoms
Stroke: focal deficit may persist after glucose correction; evaluate both if unresolved

hypoglycemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine diagnostic and hypoglycemia treatment principles.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.name: Hypothesis testing and statistical tests
hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.scope: Null and alternative hypotheses, Type I and Type II errors, statistical power, confidence intervals, p-values, t-tests (paired, unpaired), ANOVA, chi-square, Pearson correlation
hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.core: Hypothesis tests quantify incompatibility with a null model; confidence intervals describe effect estimates and uncertainty.

rows.label: Definition
items: H0: no difference/association; H1: specified difference or association
★ **α**: false-positive probability; Type I error rejects a true null
★ **β**: false-negative probability; Type II error misses a real effect

rows.label: Formula
items: Power = **1 − β**; increases with sample size, effect size, α, lower variability
95% CI ≈ estimate ± 1.96 × standard error; plausible range for true effect

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **p-value**: probability of equally/more extreme data assuming H0; not probability H0 true
95% CI excludes 0 for differences or 1 for ratios → two-sided p <0.05

rows.label: Use when
items: Pearson r: linear association between continuous variables; range −1 to +1
Ordinal/non-normal independent data → Mann–Whitney; paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Nonsignificant ≠ equivalent; statistical significance ≠ clinical importance
Repeated comparisons inflate false positives; prespecify outcomes or adjust α
Correlation neither establishes causation nor detects every nonlinear relationship

hypothesis-testing-and-statistical-tests.evidence: Statistical definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

impaired-physician.name: Impaired physician
impaired-physician.scope: Acute impairment, substance use, patient safety protection, physician health programs, mandatory reporting to state medical board
impaired-physician.core: Patient safety first when a colleague's ability to practice safely is compromised.

rows.label: Principle
items: Impairment = functional inability to practice safely from illness, substances, or cognitive decline

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Acute intoxication → stop patient contact, arrange coverage, notify supervisor immediately
★ Document objective observations and affected encounters through institutional channels
★ **Physician health program** → evaluation, treatment, monitoring, and safe return to practice

rows.label: Don't
items: Conceal unsafe care or delay intervention while seeking definitive proof
Permit impaired colleague to drive home

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Report to **state medical board** when law requires or ongoing danger remains unaddressed
PHP confidentiality and reporting exemptions vary by jurisdiction

rows.label: Traps
items: Substance use history or treatment alone ≠ current impairment
Employee assistance referral alone insufficient during an immediate patient safety threat

impaired-physician.evidence: Checked AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 9.3.2.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation and reflexes generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
Proximal weakness + ↑CK → EMG/nerve conduction (myopathic pattern); MRI guides **muscle biopsy**
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs
Guillain-Barré: ascending distal-predominant weakness, areflexia

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

inherited-bleeding-disorders.name: Inherited bleeding disorders
inherited-bleeding-disorders.scope: Hemophilia A, Hemophilia B, von Willebrand disease, factor XI deficiency, hemarthrosis, mixing studies, factor VIII inhibitors
inherited-bleeding-disorders.core: Deep tissue bleeding suggests a coagulation-factor defect; mucosal bleeding suggests platelet/von Willebrand dysfunction, even with a normal platelet count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemophilia A/B: X-linked, usually males; maternal family history may be absent
vWD usually autosomal dominant; factor XI deficiency autosomal, enriched in Ashkenazi ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **hemarthroses**, muscle hematomas and delayed postoperative bleeding → hemophilia
Epistaxis, gingival bleeding, easy bruising and heavy menses → vWD
Factor XI deficiency: variable postsurgical bleeding, especially oral/urologic procedures; hemarthrosis uncommon
Unexpected major bleeding after circumcision or surgery may reveal previously undiagnosed disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: VIII/IX/XI deficits impair intrinsic-pathway thrombin generation and fibrin stabilization
